claim: T7 phages are bound in the outermost curli polymer layers of the E. coli biofilm matrix.
source: Prior work has demonstrated that T7 phages are bound in the outermost curli polymer layers of the E. coli biofilm matrix.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work, as indicated by the reference to previous research.

claim: Matrix-trapped T7 phages remain viable and can kill colonizing cells that are T7-susceptible.
source: We show that these phages do remain viable and can kill colonizing cells that are T7-susceptible.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: If colonizing cells are present on the biofilm long enough before phage exposure, they gain phage protection via envelopment within curli-producing clusters of the resident biofilm cells.
source: However, if colonizing cells are present on the biofilm long enough before phage exposure, they gain phage protection via envelopment within curli-producing clusters of the resident biofilm cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Phages inject their genomes into the cytoplasm of their hosts.
source: Phages inject their genomes into the cytoplasm of their hosts, and in the case of obligate lytic phages, immediately begin co-opting host resources to replicate.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about phage biology.

claim: Obligate lytic phages immediately begin co-opting host resources to replicate after genome injection.
source: Phages inject their genomes into the cytoplasm of their hosts, and in the case of obligate lytic phages, immediately begin co-opting host resources to replicate.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about lytic phage behavior.

claim: Host cells are lysed to release a new cohort of phage virions.
source: Eventually, host cells are lysed to release a new cohort of phage virions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the lytic phage life cycle.

claim: Predatory pressure from phage attack drives bacterial evolution, diversification, and ultimately the community structure of many microbiomes.
source: Predatory pressure from phage attack drives bacterial evolution, diversification, and ultimately the community structure of many microbiomes (Blazanin and Turner, 2021; Harrison et al., 2013; Lenski and Levin, 1985; Abedon, 2008; Koskella and Brockhurst, 2014; Gómez and Buckling, 2011; Keen and Dantas, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Traditional phage-bacteria interaction literature mostly considers well-mixed culture conditions such as those in shaken liquids.
source: The traditional literature in this area mostly considers well-mixed culture conditions such as those in shaken liquids, which can reveal fundamental aspects of phage-bacteria interactions without spatial structure.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature based on established knowledge of the field.

claim: In nature bacteria often reside in spatially constrained, surface-bound communities, or biofilms.
source: However, in nature bacteria often reside in spatially constrained, surface-bound communities, or biofilms (Nadell et al., 2016; Hellweger et al., 2016; Flemming and Wingender, 2010; Flemming et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Phage infection in biofilm environments often produces outcomes that differ substantially from those observed in mixed liquid environments.
source: The limited work that has focused on phage infection in biofilm environments has often found outcomes that differ substantially from those observed in mixed liquid environments (Hansen et al., 2019; Levin and Bull, 2004; Simmons et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2016; Abedon, 2016; Schrag and Mittler, 1996; Eriksen et al., 2018; Simmons et al., 2018; Chaudhry et al., 2018; Pires et al., 2021; Vidakovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The biofilm matrix modulates cell-cell and cell-surface interactions.
source: A defining feature of biofilm populations is the presence of a self-secreted adhesive polymer matrix that modulates cell-cell and cell-surface interactions, in addition to influencing collective biofilm architecture (Nadell et al., 2016; Flemming and Wingender, 2010; Erskine et al., 2018; Teschler et al., 2015; Hartmann et al., 2019; Colvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The biofilm matrix influences collective biofilm architecture.
source: A defining feature of biofilm populations is the presence of a self-secreted adhesive polymer matrix that modulates cell-cell and cell-surface interactions, in addition to influencing collective biofilm architecture (Nadell et al., 2016; Flemming and Wingender, 2010; Erskine et al., 2018; Teschler et al., 2015; Hartmann et al., 2019; Colvin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pseudomonas fluorescens and Escherichia coli rapidly evolve mucoid colony phenotypes when they are under phage attack.
source: Pseudomonas fluorescens and Escherichia coli rapidly evolve mucoid colony phenotypes – which reflect increased and/or altered matrix secretion – when they are under phage attack (Scanlan and Buckling, 2012; Chaudhry et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mucoid colony phenotypes reflect increased and/or altered matrix secretion.
source: Pseudomonas fluorescens and Escherichia coli rapidly evolve mucoid colony phenotypes – which reflect increased and/or altered matrix secretion – when they are under phage attack (Scanlan and Buckling, 2012; Chaudhry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge about mucoid phenotypes.

claim: Curli fibers can block biofilm-dwelling cells from T7 and T5 phage exposure.
source: Curli fibers, a proteinaceous component of the E. coli matrix, can block biofilm-dwelling cells from T7 and T5 phage exposure (Vidakovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Phages can be seen directly enmeshed in the curli mesh without infecting biofilm cells unless the integrity of the curli layer is compromised.
source: In this case, phages can be seen directly enmeshed in the curli mesh without infecting biofilm cells unless the integrity of the curli layer is compromised (Simmons et al., 2020; Vidakovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Matrix-dependent phage protection occurs in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Recent papers by Darch et al., 2017, Díaz-Pascual et al., 2019, and Dunsing et al., 2019, respectively, suggest a similar pattern of matrix-dependent phage protection in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Vibrio cholerae, and Pantoea stewartii.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Matrix-dependent phage protection occurs in Vibrio cholerae.
source: Recent papers by Darch et al., 2017, Díaz-Pascual et al., 2019, and Dunsing et al., 2019, respectively, suggest a similar pattern of matrix-dependent phage protection in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Vibrio cholerae, and Pantoea stewartii.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Matrix-dependent phage protection occurs in Pantoea stewartii.
source: Recent papers by Darch et al., 2017, Díaz-Pascual et al., 2019, and Dunsing et al., 2019, respectively, suggest a similar pattern of matrix-dependent phage protection in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Vibrio cholerae, and Pantoea stewartii.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: If phage-exposed biofilms are disassociated by a matrix-degrading agent, the phage titer in the surrounding media increases.
source: Earlier work from Kay et al., 2011 used plaque-forming unit (PFU) count assays to show that if phage-exposed biofilms are disassociated by a matrix-degrading agent, the phage titer in the surrounding media increases, suggesting that phages released from the matrix are potentially still infectious.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Phages released from the matrix are potentially still infectious.
source: Earlier work from Kay et al., 2011 used plaque-forming unit (PFU) count assays to show that if phage-exposed biofilms are disassociated by a matrix-degrading agent, the phage titer in the surrounding media increases, suggesting that phages released from the matrix are potentially still infectious.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research findings.

claim: E. coli produces flagellar filaments during biofilm formation.
source: E. coli produces a variety of matrix components at different times during biofilm formation, including flagellar filaments, curli amyloid fibers, and polysaccharides such as colanic acid and cellulose (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Beloin et al., 2008; Barnhart and Chapman, 2006; Evans and Chapman, 2014; Hammar et al., 1996; Pesavento et al., 2008; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: E. coli produces curli amyloid fibers during biofilm formation.
source: E. coli produces a variety of matrix components at different times during biofilm formation, including flagellar filaments, curli amyloid fibers, and polysaccharides such as colanic acid and cellulose (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Beloin et al., 2008; Barnhart and Chapman, 2006; Evans and Chapman, 2014; Hammar et al., 1996; Pesavento et al., 2008; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: E. coli produces polysaccharides such as colanic acid and cellulose during biofilm formation.
source: E. coli produces a variety of matrix components at different times during biofilm formation, including flagellar filaments, curli amyloid fibers, and polysaccharides such as colanic acid and cellulose (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Beloin et al., 2008; Barnhart and Chapman, 2006; Evans and Chapman, 2014; Hammar et al., 1996; Pesavento et al., 2008; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Curli fibers are the single matrix component known to be essential for T7 phage protection in E. coli biofilms.
source: Curli fibers are the single matrix component known to be essential for T7 phage protection in E. coli biofilms (Vidakovic et al., 2018) and are assembled by extracellular polymerization of CsgA monomers on an outer membrane baseplate comprised of CsgB (Evans and Chapman, 2014; Barnhart and Chapman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Curli fibers are assembled by extracellular polymerization of CsgA monomers on an outer membrane baseplate comprised of CsgB.
source: Curli fibers are the single matrix component known to be essential for T7 phage protection in E. coli biofilms (Vidakovic et al., 2018) and are assembled by extracellular polymerization of CsgA monomers on an outer membrane baseplate comprised of CsgB (Evans and Chapman, 2014; Barnhart and Chapman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Curli proteins secreted by E. coli localize primarily in the upper half of the biofilm-dwelling population.
source: Curli proteins secreted by E. coli localize primarily in the upper half of the biofilm-dwelling population, and introduced phages become trapped in the outer part of this curli matrix layer (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Introduced phages become trapped in the outer part of the curli matrix layer.
source: Curli proteins secreted by E. coli localize primarily in the upper half of the biofilm-dwelling population, and introduced phages become trapped in the outer part of this curli matrix layer (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Biofilm-dwelling cells amongst and below the curli fiber matrix layer become protected against T7 exposure in the absence of the evolution of physiological resistance to T7 phages.
source: The biofilm-dwelling cells amongst and below the curli fiber matrix layer thus become protected against T7 exposure in the absence of the evolution of physiological resistance to T7 phages (Simmons et al., 2020; Vidakovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Resident biofilms were grown for 62 hr to achieve optimal curli expression along the biofilm front.
source: We first grew biofilms of E. coli AR3110 for 62 hr (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1); prior work has established this growth period as optimal for full curli expression along the biofilm front (Vidakovic et al., 2018), and we confirmed this result in our microfluidic growth conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and experimental confirmation shown in figures.

claim: Resident cells harbored a chromosomal construct for constitutive expression of the far-red fluorescent protein mKate2.
source: The resident cells harbored a chromosomal construct for constitutive expression of the far-red fluorescent protein mKate2 (Shcherbo et al., 2007) to make them visible with fluorescence time-lapse microscopy.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Biofilms were exposed to a 1 hr pulse of media containing lytic T7 phages at 2x10^8 PFU/mL.
source: The biofilms were then exposed to a 1 hr pulse of media containing lytic T7 phages at 2x108 PFU/mL, such that phages could accumulate in the outer matrix curli layer (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The phages contained a sfGFP expression construct engineered into their genome.
source: The phages contained a sfGFP (Pédelacq et al., 2006) expression construct engineered into their genome, allowing us to visualize any cells that became phage-infected (Vidakovic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: In the absence of phages, resident biofilms could be colonized by planktonic cells, albeit not at high efficiency.
source: We found that in the absence of phage exposure, resident biofilms could be colonized by planktonic cells, albeit not at high efficiency (Figure 1E,I).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Colonizing cells were restricted to the outer surface of the resident biofilms and could not enter the biofilm interior.
source: The colonizing cells were restricted to the outer surface of the resident biofilms and could not enter the biofilm interior, similar to what we have seen previously for V. cholerae (Nadell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data and comparison to prior work.

claim: When resident biofilms were pre-exposed to phages, colonization by phage-susceptible cells was almost completely eliminated.
source: However, when resident biofilms were pre-exposed to phages, colonization by phage-susceptible cells was almost completely eliminated (Figure 1F,I).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Most invading cells detected on phage-exposed biofilms were fluorescent in the sfGFP channel, indicating that they had been phage-infected but not yet lysed.
source: Further, most invading cells that were detected on phage-exposed biofilms were fluorescent in the sfGFP channel, indicating that they had been phage-infected but not yet lysed.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data and inference from the fluorescence signal.

claim: Susceptible invading cells encounter phages in the curli matrix, become infected, and lyse to release new phages, or fail to divide further.
source: Our interpretation of this result is that susceptible invading cells encounter phages in the curli matrix, become infected, and lyse to release new phages, or fail to divide further.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: Without phage pre-exposure, there were numerous instances of cell clusters with 20 cells or more, indicating several rounds of division in the 10 hr between invasion and imaging.
source: Without pre-exposure, we found numerous instances of cell clusters with 20 cells or more, indicating several rounds of division in the 10 hr between invasion and imaging (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: On biofilms exposed to phages prior to invasion of new E. coli cells, there were almost no groups larger than one or a few cells.
source: On biofilms exposed to phages prior to invasion of new E. coli cells, there were almost no groups larger than one or a few cells (Figure 1K), indicating few or no divisions in the period between invasion and imaging.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The ΔtrxA deletion mutant does not allow for phage amplification.
source: We tested this possibility by repeating the experiment above with invading cultures of an E. coli mutant harboring a clean deletion of trxA; this strain does not allow for phage amplification (Qimron et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The ΔtrxA deletion mutant invaded resident biofilms at equal rates whether or not the resident was pre-exposed to T7 phages.
source: The ΔtrxA deletion mutant was found to invade resident biofilms at equal rates whether or not the resident was pre-exposed to T7 phages, which suggests that phages do not block attachment sites for invading cells (Figure 1G,H,I).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Phages do not block attachment sites for invading cells.
source: The ΔtrxA deletion mutant was found to invade resident biofilms at equal rates whether or not the resident was pre-exposed to T7 phages, which suggests that phages do not block attachment sites for invading cells (Figure 1G,H,I).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The ΔtrxA deletion mutant undergoes abortive infection upon exposure to phage T7.
source: Noting that the ΔtrxA deletion mutant undergoes abortive infection upon exposure to phage T7, the fact that ΔtrxA can colonize resident biofilms, while WT E. coli cannot, indicates that phage amplification from initial sites of infection may be important for elimination of phage-susceptible invading cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ΔtrxA mutant phenotype.

claim: Phage amplification from initial sites of infection may be important for elimination of phage-susceptible invading cells.
source: Noting that the ΔtrxA deletion mutant undergoes abortive infection upon exposure to phage T7, the fact that ΔtrxA can colonize resident biofilms, while WT E. coli cannot, indicates that phage amplification from initial sites of infection may be important for elimination of phage-susceptible invading cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results comparing WT and ΔtrxA mutant.

claim: Phages that are trapped in the curli matrix of E. coli biofilms are persistent as a threat to incoming susceptible bacteria.
source: Phages that are trapped in the curli matrix of E. coli biofilms are thus persistent as a threat to incoming susceptible bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Curli-protected cells within resident biofilms that disperse may be susceptible to phages that are released from the biofilm exterior.
source: This result also implies that in the event that curli-protected cells within resident biofilms disperse individually or en masse, they may too be susceptible to phages that are released from the biofilm exterior.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Invading cells were mostly killed by T7 phage exposure when phage pulses occurred immediately after biofilms were colonized by an invading strain.
source: When phage pulses occurred immediately after biofilms were colonized by an invading strain, the invading cells were mostly killed by T7 phage exposure (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Invading cells were not significantly affected by phage pulses that arrived 10 hr after the colonizing strain attached to the resident biofilm outer periphery.
source: Interestingly, however, invading cells were not significantly affected by phage pulses that arrived 10 hr after the colonizing strain attached to the resident biofilm outer periphery (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: When invading cells harbored the His-labeled variant of csgA, negligible anti-His fluorescence was detected in the 10 hr following invasion of the biofilm exterior.
source: When invading cells harbored the His-labeled variant of csgA, we detected negligible anti-His fluorescence in the 10 hr following invasion of the biofilm exterior (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: When cells in the resident biofilm harbored the His-labeled variant of csgA, abundant anti-His staining was detectable in the upper surface of the resident biofilm.
source: By contrast, when cells in the resident biofilm harbored the His-labeled variant of csgA, abundant anti-His staining was detectable in the upper surface of the resident biofilm (Figure 3B–F), including the surroundings of the colonizing cells (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations.

claim: Invading cells do not gain phage protection in the 10 hr following colonization because they produce their own curli fibers, but rather because they coopt the curli fibers being produced by cells in the resident biofilm.
source: These two observations indicate that invading cells do not gain phage protection in the 10 hr following colonization because they produce their own curli fibers, but rather because they coopt the curli fibers being produced by cells in the resident biofilm (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: At the 10 hr mark, invading cells were surrounded by the same amount of curli as the resident strain at the beginning of the invasion experiment.
source: At the 10 hr mark, invading cells were surrounded by the same amount of curli as the resident strain at the beginning of the invasion experiment.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by image analysis of curli accumulation.

claim: Despite lacking CsgB curli baseplates, invaders were still protected after a 10-hr delay prior to phage exposure in the system.
source: However, despite lacking CsgB curli baseplates, invaders were still protected after a 10-hr delay prior to phage exposure in the system (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Invading cells do not have to be able to directly polymerize CsgA on their exterior to gain phage protection over the 10 hr after attaching to the biofilm surface.
source: This prompted the interpretation that invading cells do not have to be able to directly polymerize CsgA on their exterior to gain phage protection over the 10 hr after attaching to the biofilm surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: Invading cells indirectly coopt curli produced by the resident biofilm by becoming sufficiently enveloped amidst clusters of resident cells that their exposure to incoming phages is greatly reduced or eliminated.
source: Rather this result suggests that the invading cells – despite remaining distinct physiologically from the resident cells by virtue of not producing CsgA or CsgB themselves – indirectly coopt curli produced by the resident biofilm by becoming sufficiently enveloped amidst clusters of resident cells that their exposure to incoming phages is greatly reduced or eliminated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on inference.

claim: Matrix-embedded T7 phages can remain infectious on the curli-protected E. coli biofilm surface and kill newly arriving susceptible bacteria.
source: We have shown that matrix-embedded T7 phages can remain infectious on the curli-protected E. coli biofilm surface and kill newly arriving susceptible bacteria.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Biofilm-dwelling microbes, by trapping phages on the biofilm periphery, can incidentally weaponize them against incoming phage-susceptible cells.
source: In this sense, biofilm-dwelling microbes, by trapping phages on the biofilm periphery, can incidentally weaponize them against incoming phage-susceptible cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: If invading E. coli cells attach to a resident biofilm and have sufficient time to become entangled in the curli matrix, they gain protection from subsequent phage exposure.
source: On the other hand, we found that if invading E. coli cells attach to a resident biofilm and have sufficient time to become entangled in the curli matrix, they too gain protection from subsequent phage exposure.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Protection from phage exposure is obtained by indirect exploitation of the resident biofilm's curli matrix.
source: This protection is obtained by indirect exploitation of the resident biofilm's curli matrix: invading cells did not significantly use resident-produced curli monomers to polymerize curli on their own exterior, but rather became sufficiently enveloped in curli-producing groups of resident biofilm cells that they were no longer exposed to an incoming phage attack.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Phages trapped in host mucosal linings can kill incoming bacteria.
source: Our observations bear an interesting analogy to those of Barr et al., 2013, who found that phages trapped in host mucosal linings can kill incoming bacteria (see also Barr et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Phage entrapment and their blocking effect against bacterial colonization is important not just in host associated mucosal environments but even more broadly to many biofilm contexts.
source: We speculate on the basis of our results here that phage entrapment and their blocking effect against bacterial colonization is important not just in host associated mucosal environments but even more broadly to many biofilm contexts in which phage-trapping matrix material could potentially influence the pattern of community succession.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental results.

claim: The biofilm matrix almost certainly evolved in part to protect the cells within from external threats, including exposure to phages.
source: But the biofilm matrix almost certainly did evolve in part to protect the cells within from external threats, including exposure to phages; when phages are trapped in the matrix and remain viable, they can subsequently influence whether other incoming bacteria (depending on their phage susceptibility) colonize the resident biofilm surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge and the experimental results.

claim: When phages are trapped in the matrix and remain viable, they can subsequently influence whether other incoming bacteria colonize the resident biofilm surface.
source: But the biofilm matrix almost certainly did evolve in part to protect the cells within from external threats, including exposure to phages; when phages are trapped in the matrix and remain viable, they can subsequently influence whether other incoming bacteria (depending on their phage susceptibility) colonize the resident biofilm surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Biofilm colonization by susceptible cells was effectively eliminated by the presence of phages on the biofilm surface.
source: As a demonstration of principle, we studied here the effect of matrix-embedded T7 phages on the colonization ability of cells isogenic to those in the resident E. coli biofilm, showing that biofilm colonization by susceptible cells was effectively eliminated by the presence of phages on the biofilm surface.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: E. coli strains used in these experiments were all derived from E. coli AR3110.
source: E. coli strains used in these experiments were all derived from E. coli AR3110 and are listed in Table 1 below.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Each strain used for imaging contained a codon-optimized fluorescent protein construct under the control of a constitutive Ptaq promoter.
source: Each strain used for imaging contained a codon-optimized fluorescent protein construct (mKO-κ, mKate2 or mTFP1) under the control of a constitutive Ptaq promoter.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Fluorescent protein constructs were inserted using the traditional lambda-red recombineering method.
source: Fluorescent protein constructs were inserted using the traditional lambda-red recombineering method by amplifying constructs with primer overhangs corresponding to the attB site (Datsenko and Wanner, 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: E. coli AR3110 was used due to its strong biofilm formation ability relative to other K12 domesticated lab strains of E. coli.
source: E. coli AR3110 was used due to its strong biofilm formation ability relative to other K12 domesticated lab strains of E. coli, and the literature history of establishing the timing and components of matrix expression in this strain background (Simmons et al., 2020; Vidakovic et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2013a; Serra et al., 2013b; Serra and Hengge, 2014).
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental design based on established knowledge and citations.

claim: His-labeling of CsgA has been shown previously not to influence curli function in live biofilms.
source: His-labeling of CsgA has been shown previously not to influence curli function in live biofilms (Vidakovic et al., 2018; Serra et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.
